Subject: Reserved capacity question — monthly close headroom

Hi Soojin,

Thanks again for the demo last week — the dedicated pool walkthrough was helpful. As we dig into procurement, theres one operational item we need clarity on: our month-end processing spikes. During close windows (typically last 48 hours of the month) our token throughput jumps ~3–4x for short bursts.

Were evaluating Reserved GPU commitments but need an SLA carveout that guarantees a minimum of baseline throughput during those windows (or a defined headroom policy + credits if not met). Specifically:
- Can Redwood commit to X tokens/sec per reserved GPU at 95th percentile under normal load?
- How does queueing and preemption behave when the platform is under contended load?
- If a dedicated pool is preempted for higher-priority workloads, what crediting mechanism is available?

Attached: Cypher_Prod_Telemetry_June.pdf (high-level traffic curves). Procurement is looped on this thread (procurement@cypherlytics.com) — theyll want wording for contract redlines.

Looking for a short call or a draft carveout we can review with legal.

Best,

Soojin / Amelia — adding the technical constraints so the carveout is concrete. Key points from runtime:

1) Throughput baseline: for a "reserved GPU" we typically model token throughput as a function of model size and batch composition. For a 32GB A100-like reservation the conservative baseline is ~12k tokens/sec under steady-state batching; for burst windows we can sustain 50% higher for short durations with elastic prefetching. We should state throughput in tokens/sec or p99 tokens/ms equivalently.

2) Queueing behavior: Dedicated pools use per-tenant queues with fairness tokens; during contended periods low-latency routes get priority. Preemption is implemented as graceful eviction of burst-ephemeral workers with a 30–90s drain depending on in-flight requests. That means tail latency can spike if large KV caches are invalidated mid-flight.

3) Headroom policy options (pick one):
  a) Reserved headroom carveout: hold N GPUs in a non-preemptible state for scheduled windows (hard guarantee),
  b) Conditional headroom: provide soft guarantees with crediting if median throughput drops below threshold,
  c) Burst pool with soft-preemption but minimum preservation (e.g., preserve 60% of baseline tokens/sec).

4) Crediting formula (example): 1 day of credits for each 4 hours where mean throughput < 75% of committed baseline during a scheduled window.

Ive attached a short playbook with queueing flow (queueing_playbook.txt) and a tentative technical paragraph you can drop into an SLA. Happy to scope numbers further on a call.

— Ben Carter
Director, Solutions Engineering
Redwood Inference

Theyve also asked for a short redline to drop into our PO. I can get legals availability next week for a 30-minute call.

Amelia — quick alignment from infra/SDR side: we can offer a hybrid that hits procurements predictability ask while limiting cost exposure. Proposed text (draft SLA clause):

"Reserved Capacity Headroom: Redwood will reserve up to 2 non-preemptible devices for Customer during mutually agreed scheduled windows ("Close Windows"). Reserved devices will provide a baseline throughput of 10,000 tokens/second per device for the model series specified by Customer. If measured mean throughput across the Close Window falls below 95% of the committed baseline, Customer will be eligible for service credits. Service crediting will be calculated as 0.5 days of prepaid reserved capacity credit for each hour where mean throughput < 95% baseline, subject to a maximum credit cap equal to 30 days of reserved capacity in any rolling 12-month period."

This approach preserves deterministic capacity for scheduled windows, keeps preemption behavior predictable elsewhere, and gives us a documented crediting formula.

If that number (10k tokens/sec) is too aggressive/ conservative for your workload we can rebench in the 30-day pilot and update the clause. Lauren / Legal can prep a redline.

— Marcus Lin
Principal Infra Engineer, Redwood Inference
